extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism (poets, playwrights, literature students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing and judging tragic and epic poetry (and related genres), focusing on imitation (medium, objects, manner), the parts of a poem/plot, diction, music, spectacle, and genre-specific requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose tragedy as enacted action (not merely told). Ensure the action is elevated and unified, use appropriate poetic ornament (rhythm, harmony, song) in different parts, and aim for catharsis (pity and fear leading to proper purgation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (and contrast with History)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry and Tragedy agree in unity of action—i.e., the poem should represent a single connected action—this is contrasted with mere historical narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the plot so all episodes contribute to one coherent action; avoid digressive or episodic sequences that break the unity. Prefer a tight causal chain rather than a collection of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal Limits of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (a single day), or but slightly to exceed this limit, while Epic action has no limits of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing tragedy aim for a compact temporal span (approximately one day) to preserve dramatic intensity and unity; reserve expansive temporal scope for epic/narrative forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot / Structure (the requisite structure of a good poem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the plot is requisite to a good poem; tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude—plot concerns the number and nature of parts, episodes, and the arrangement of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the plot a connected whole with a clear beginning, middle, and end. Arrange episodes so causes lead to effects; use reversals and recognitions where appropriate to produce emotional impact. Avoid disconnected or merely episodic organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action implies personal agents who necessarily possess distinctive qualities both of character and thought; modes of imitation will portray men either better than in real life, worse, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose qualities (virtues, faults) are consistent and appropriate to the action; choose moral types appropriate to genre (tragedy: better/noble types; comedy: worse/meaner types). Character actions should drive the plot logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) / Intellectual Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is revealed in the dramatic speeches composed according to the rules of Rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express argument, reasoning, and the play's intellectual content through rhetorically well-formed speeches. Thought should be coherent, persuasive, and aligned with character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Poetic Diction (Lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (language) covers the words and modes of speech admissible in poetry, including the use of metaphor; diction combines elevation of language with perspicuity. Diction itself largely falls within the domain of delivery, though poetic diction has specific allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words and figures (metaphor etc.) that are elevated yet clear. Avoid grotesque or inappropriate colloquialisms when a stately manner is required; ensure diction serves both the aesthetic (elevation) and intelligibility (perspicuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody / Song / Musical Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is to be embellished with rhythm, 'harmony,' and song; some parts are rendered through verse alone, others with the aid of song. In music (flute/lyre) harmony and rhythm are employed—dancing uses rhythm alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate rhythm, musicality, and song into parts of the work where appropriate. Where song or musical accompaniment is used, ensure it is organically related to the dramatic action and enhances emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus / Choral Odes as Organic Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus so its odes and interventions contribute meaningfully to the plot, mood, or thematic development, rather than serving as mere interludes or interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Scenic Display / Opsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since tragic imitation implies persons acting, spectacular equipment (scenic display) will be a part of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include spectacle as an element that supports the imitation, but ensure it serves the action; spectacle should not substitute for dramatic structure or character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Mixing Genre-Appropriate Details (No Epic Overcharge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to 'overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist inserting epic-scale detail, digressions, or sprawling narration into tragedy. Keep the tragic mode focused, concise, and suited to dramatic enactment rather than epic elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediums of Imitation (Rhythm, Language, Harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts differ in their medium: imitation is produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony,' either singly or combined; some arts employ all three (e.g., Tragedy, Comedy), some one or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate medium(s) for your genre: combine rhythm/language/music where the form calls for it; use purely verbal imitation for prose or verse without music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of Imitation (Narration vs Presenting Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration—speaking in another person or in his own—or he may present all his characters as living and moving before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic 'showing' (characters enacted) for drama to maximize immediacy; use narrative distance for epic or when the narrator's perspective is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Imitation / Moral Types
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the objects of imitation are men in action, these must be represented either as better than in real life, worse, or as they are; genres favor different portrayals (Tragedy makes men better; Comedy makes men worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the moral framing early: make characters consistently more noble (tragedy) or more flawed (comedy), or realistic as suits the poem's aims, and let that choice inform tone and incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic Poetry Requirements and Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry agrees with Tragedy in unity of action but differs in (1) the length of the poem, (2) the metre (typically one kind, hexameter), and (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction; Epic is narrative and not temporally confined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing epic, plan for large scope and narrative treatment, consistent metre (hexameter), freedom of temporal span, and techniques to lend plausibility to improbable events (poetic truth and verisimilitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Truth / Answering Critical Objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections to poetry are answered by elucidating the meaning of Poetic Truth and its difference from common reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize poetic plausibility and thematic or moral truth over literal factual accuracy; anticipate objections by distinguishing poetic conventions from everyday reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre Choice for Dialogue and Colloquial Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Once dialogue had come in, the iambic measure replaced trochaic tetrameter because the iambic is, of all measures, the most colloquial—conversational speech runs into iambic lines more frequently than into other kinds of verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iambic or colloquial-appropriate metres for dialogue and conversational passages to achieve natural-sounding speech; reserve elevated or narrative metres for other functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific Tone and Diction (Stately vs Grotesque)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grotesque diction of the earlier satyric form gave way to the stately manner of Tragedy; diction should suit the genre's tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a stately, elevated diction for high genres (tragedy/epic); avoid satyric or grotesque diction except where genre or effect specifically require it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and Development of Dramatic Devices (actors, scene-painting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical developments: Aeschylus introduced a second actor (diminishing Chorus importance), Sophocles raised actors to three and added scene-painting; dialogue eventually took the leading part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ actors, staging, and scene-painting to facilitate dramatic enactment and dialogue; emphasize spoken interaction over choral dominance to foreground character and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Bounds of Comedy (Ludicrous vs Painful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of characters of a lower type—the Ludicrous is merely a subdivision of the ugly and consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing comedy, target defects or ugliness that provoke laughter without real harm; keep the tone within the bounds of the ludicrous rather than the tragic or painful.
